# Where we are

Last week you built a measurement instrument.

You wrote a prompt, ran it on a sample, compared it to human labels, and computed
accuracy.

--

<br>

Today we use that variable.

---

# Table of contents

1. [The situation you are now in](#setup)

2. [Generated regressors: the general problem](#core)

3. [Why "it's just attenuation" is wrong](#attenuation)

4. [A worked example](#worked)

5. [The corrections](#corrections)

6. [The design lesson](#design)

7. [Training-data leakage](#leakage)

8. [Silicon sampling](#silicon)

9. [Writing the measurement section](#writing)

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: setup

# The situation you are now in

---

# You did everything right

You have 50,000 product reviews.

You wrote a careful prompt that classifies each one as complaining about *product
quality* versus something else.

--

You hand-labeled 500 of them yourself. You checked inter-rater reliability with an RA.

--

<br>

Your LLM agrees with the gold standard **87% of the time**.

--

<br>

Precision 0.85. Recall 0.89. Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.74.

---

# You are pleased

That is a better agreement rate than most two-human coding studies report. And better
than the sentiment dictionaries this literature ran on for fifteen years.

--

<br>

You run the LLM on all 50,000 reviews. You now have a variable.

--

<br>

You put it in a regression.

---

# The regression

$$y_i = \alpha + \beta \, \widehat{D}_i + X_i'\gamma + \varepsilon_i$$

where $\widehat{D}_i$ is the LLM's label and $D_i$ is the truth you cannot observe at
scale.

--

<br>

You get $\hat\beta = 0.31$, standard error 0.04, $t = 7.8$.

--

<br>

You write it up.

---

# The question

Your instrument is 87% accurate.

--

<br>

.large2[Is your regression 87% right?]

--

<br>

No. There is no theorem connecting classification accuracy to the properties of a
downstream estimator.

--

<br>

87% accuracy is consistent with $\hat\beta$ being nearly unbiased. It is also consistent
with $\hat\beta$ having the **wrong sign**. Accuracy alone cannot distinguish those two
cases.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: core

# The core result

---

# First, the general version

Nothing I am about to say is about LLMs.

--

<br>

.large2[If a variable in your regression was **estimated** rather than **observed**, the
regression inherits that estimation error.]

--

<br>

Econometrics has a name for this: the **generated regressor** problem. Pagan (1984);
Murphy & Topel (1985).

---

# You have already met it

You have used generated regressors without calling them that:

--

- predicted probabilities from a first-stage model
- propensity scores
- factor scores and principal components
- fitted values from a first stage in 2SLS
- any index someone built for you and you took as data

--

<br>

And the pre-LLM version of exactly today's problem: **a research assistant who codes your
variable at 85% accuracy.**

---

# The same is true of every classifier

The result holds for **any** imperfect predictor:

--

.small90[
| | |
|:--|:--|
| a fine-tuned BERT model | a random forest |
| a lasso | a keyword dictionary |
| a hand-coded RA | an LLM |
]

--

<br>

The papers say so explicitly. Egami et al. call them "imperfect **surrogates**."
Battaglia et al.: "variables generated by AI **or machine learning**." Prediction-powered
inference assumes nothing at all about the algorithm.

--

<br>

.large2[If you file this as "a thing about LLMs," you will not recognize it when a paper
uses a random forest.]

---

# So why is this lecture about LLMs?

Because the problem went from **rare** to **everywhere**.

--

<br>

Almost nobody hand-coded 200,000 documents. It was too expensive, so the studies that
needed it did not get done.

--

Now everybody can. The constraint that kept this problem uncommon is gone.

---

# Four things that are genuinely new

**1. No labeled data by default.** Supervised machine learning hands you a training set by
construction. Zero-shot annotation does not, the gold standard is now an act of will.

--

**2. Illegible error structure.** You know what is in a lasso's feature set. You cannot
reason about what drives an LLM's mistakes. You can only measure them.

--

**3. Prompt sensitivity** as a researcher degree of freedom. No clean pre-LLM analogue.

--

**4. Non-reproducibility.** You can seed a random forest. You cannot pin a model version
forever.

---

# And one thing that is a real extension

The classical literature assumes the first stage is **consistently estimated**. Given
that, the corrections are mostly about getting standard errors right.

--

<br>

An LLM classifier is not a consistent estimator of anything.

--

<br>

.large2[Which is why the modern papers advertise working with **arbitrarily biased**
surrogates.]

--

That is a genuine extension of the old problem, not a re-run of it.

---

# Now the result

.large2[Plugging model-generated labels into a downstream regression gives you **biased
coefficients** and **invalid confidence intervals**, even when the labels are highly
accurate.]

--

<br>

.small90[Egami, Hinck, Stewart & Wei (2023), "Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream
Inference: Design-Based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of Large
Language Models," *NeurIPS* 36.]

---

# Unpack "invalid confidence intervals"

Two separate failures. People conflate them.

--

**Bias.** $\hat\beta$ does not converge to $\beta$. Your point estimate is wrong.

--

**Coverage.** Your 95% CI does not contain $\beta$ 95% of the time. Often far less.

--

<br>

The second is worse in a specific way: your standard errors reflect sampling uncertainty
in $y$, and nothing else.

--

They do not know that $\widehat{D}$ is an estimate.

---

# Your standard errors are lying

You have two sources of uncertainty:

1. Sampling variation, the usual one, the one `lm()` reports
2. Measurement uncertainty, $\widehat{D}_i \neq D_i$, and you don't know where

--

<br>

The plug-in regression accounts for the first and treats the second as if it did not
exist.

--

<br>

.large2[The software has no way to know your regressor was generated.]

--

To `lm()`, `llm_label` is a column of ones and zeros like any other.

---

# More data makes this worse

With $n = 500$, your standard errors are wide enough that the measurement bias might hide
inside them.

--

With $n = 50{,}000$, your standard errors shrink toward zero. And the bias does not.

--

<br>

Classification error does not average out as $n$ grows. It is not noise. It is a
**feature of the instrument**, and it persists in the probability limit.

--

<br>

.large2[You converge, with great confidence, to the wrong number.]

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: attenuation

# Why "it's just attenuation" is wrong

---

# The objection I always get

Here is the response, and I get it every single time I present this.

--

<br>

> "Sure, there's measurement error. But measurement error in a regressor causes
> **attenuation**. My estimate is biased toward zero. So my result is *conservative*
> if I find an effect despite the noise, the true effect is even bigger."

--

<br>

This is a good objection. It is what your first-year econometrics course taught you.

--

<br>

.large2[It is wrong here.]

---

# What the textbook actually says

Classical measurement error:

$$\widehat{D}_i = D_i + u_i$$

--

with the classical assumptions:

- $u_i$ has mean zero
- $u_i \perp D_i$
- $u_i \perp X_i$
- $u_i \perp \varepsilon_i$

--

<br>

Under **those** assumptions, in a bivariate regression:

$$\text{plim } \hat\beta = \beta \cdot \frac{\sigma^2_D}{\sigma^2_D + \sigma^2_u} \;<\; \beta$$

--

Attenuation. Toward zero. Always.

---

# Look at the assumptions again

$$u_i \perp D_i \qquad u_i \perp X_i \qquad u_i \perp \varepsilon_i$$

--

<br>

Every one of these fails for an LLM classifier.

--

<br>

Not "might fail in edge cases." **Fails, structurally, by construction.**

---

# Failure 1: the error cannot be mean-zero

$D_i \in \{0,1\}$ and $\widehat{D}_i \in \{0,1\}$.

--

So $u_i = \widehat{D}_i - D_i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$.

--

<br>

If $D_i = 1$, the error can only be $0$ or $-1$.

If $D_i = 0$, the error can only be $0$ or $+1$.

--

<br>

.large2[The error is mechanically correlated with the truth.]

--

This is the **binary variable** problem, known long before LLMs (Aigner 1973). Even
symmetric misclassification in a binary regressor breaks the classical model.

---

# Failure 2: the error is correlated with $X$

This is the one that matters, and it is specific to what LLMs are.

--

<br>

An LLM does not make errors at random.

--

<br>

.large2[It fails on the cases that are **hard**.]

---

# What "hard" means

Hard cases are:

- sarcastic
- ambiguous
- domain-specific jargon
- mixed sentiment
- unusually short, or unusually long
- written by an atypical author
- from an underrepresented subgroup
- about an unfamiliar product category

--

<br>

Now the question that makes this a research problem:

--

<br>

.large2[Is "hard for the LLM" independent of your treatment?]

---

# Almost never

The cases the model finds hard are hard **because they are substantively distinctive**.

--

<br>

And substantively distinctive is usually exactly the thing you are studying.

--

<br>

- Studying a policy change? The affected units are the unusual ones.
- Studying a new product category? The model has seen less of it.
- Studying an underrepresented group? The model is worse on their text.
- Studying reactions to a shock? Shock-period language is atypical.

--

<br>

.large2[Your treatment and the model's error rate are correlated because they are driven
by the same thing.]

---

# What breaks

Once $\text{Cov}(u_i, X_i) \neq 0$, the attenuation result does not apply.

--

<br>

Non-classical measurement error in a regressor gives bias of **arbitrary sign and
magnitude**.

--

- Toward zero
- Away from zero
- Across zero
- Larger in absolute value than $\beta$ itself

--

<br>

.large2["Conservative" is not available to you.]

---

# Why this is not pedantry

If bias is toward zero, you can write in your paper:

> "Measurement error attenuates our estimates, so the reported coefficients are a lower
> bound on the true effect."

--

Referees accept this. It is a real argument. It is the argument the entire measurement
error literature was built to license.

--

<br>

**You cannot make it.**

--

<br>

If you write that sentence with an LLM-generated regressor, and I am your referee, that
is where I stop reading and start writing the report.

---

# The other half: error in $y$

"Fine, I'll put the LLM variable on the left-hand side. Measurement error in the
*dependent* variable is benign."

--

<br>

In the classical setup, yes:

$$\widehat{y}_i = y_i + u_i \quad\Rightarrow\quad \widehat{y}_i = \alpha + \beta X_i + (\varepsilon_i + u_i)$$

--

If $u_i \perp X_i$, $\hat\beta$ is unbiased. You just lose precision.

--

<br>

Look at the condition. $u_i \perp X_i$.

---

# Same failure, same place

$u_i \perp X_i$ is exactly the assumption that fails.

--

<br>

The LLM misclassifies the outcome more often in the treated group, because treated
documents are distinctive.

--

That is a treatment-correlated shift in the measured outcome.

--

<br>

.large2[That is not noise. That is a treatment effect you invented.]

--

<br>

Moving the generated variable from the right side to the left side does not save you.

---

# Summary of this section

| | Classical ME | LLM classification error |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $E[u] = 0$ | assumed | fails (binary) |
| $u \perp D$ | assumed | fails (binary) |
| $u \perp X$ | assumed | **fails (hardness)** |
| Bias in $\hat\beta$ (regressor) | toward zero | any direction |
| Bias in $\hat\beta$ (outcome) | none | any direction |
| Correct SEs from `lm()` | yes | no |

--

<br>

The row in bold is the one that does the damage.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: worked

# A worked example

---

# The setup

You study whether a platform's **verified purchase badge** changes what people write.

--

Treatment: $X_i = 1$ if the review is from a verified purchaser.

Outcome: $D_i = 1$ if the review is **negative**.

--

<br>

You have no human labels at scale, so you use a classifier. It happens to be an LLM;
nothing below depends on that.

--

<br>

Let's make up numbers. Small ones. Follow them.

---

# The truth

10,000 reviews. Half verified, half not.

.small90[
| | Unverified ($X=0$) | Verified ($X=1$) |
|:--|--:|--:|
| $n$ | 5,000 | 5,000 |
| Truly negative | 1,500 | 1,000 |
| True rate | **30%** | **20%** |
]

--

<br>

True effect: verified purchasers are **10 percentage points** less likely to write a
negative review.

--

$$\beta = -0.10$$

--

That is the number you want.

---

# The classifier's weakness

It handles plain negative reviews fine.

It fails on **sarcasm**, "great, another broken hinge, love it" gets labeled positive.
An RA skimming 500 reviews an hour makes the same mistake.

--

<br>

Now the substantive fact that ruins everything:

--

<br>

.large2[Unverified reviewers write sarcastically. Verified purchasers write plainly.]

--

<br>

Plausible? Yes. Unverified reviews skew toward performative, entertainment-oriented
writing. That is a real thing about that population.

---

# Put numbers on it

Among the truly negative reviews:

.small90[
| | Unverified | Verified |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Truly negative | 1,500 | 1,000 |
| Of which sarcastic | 600 (40%) | 100 (10%) |
| Missed (all sarcasm) | 600 | 100 |
| Labeled negative | 900 | 900 |
]

--

<br>

Assume it makes no other errors. No false positives. Perfect on everything plain.

---

# The accuracy looks great

Total errors: $600 + 100 = 700$ out of 10,000.

--

<br>

.large2[Accuracy = **93%**.]

--

<br>

You would report that number with confidence. It is higher than the 87% we started with.

--

Any referee would accept 93%.

---

# Now run the regression

.small90[
| | Unverified | Verified |
|:--|--:|--:|
| **True** negative rate | 30% | 20% |
| **Measured** negative rate | 18% | 18% |
]

--

<br>

$$\hat\beta = 0.18 - 0.18 = 0.00$$

--

<br>

.large2[True effect: $-0.10$. Estimated effect: $0.00$.]

--

<br>

93% accuracy. The entire effect is gone.

---

# And it gets worse

Push the sarcasm gap a little. Say 50% of unverified negatives are sarcastic, 5% of
verified negatives are.

--

.small90[
| | Unverified | Verified |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Truly negative | 1,500 | 1,000 |
| Sarcastic (missed) | 750 | 50 |
| Labeled negative | 750 | 950 |
| Measured negative rate | 15% | 19% |
]

--

<br>

$$\hat\beta = 0.19 - 0.15 = +0.04$$

--

<br>

.large2[The sign flipped.]

---

# What just happened

Accuracy stayed around 92%.

The estimate moved from $-0.10$ to $0.00$ to $+0.04$.

--

<br>

Nothing about the model got worse. The only thing that changed is **how the model's
errors line up with the treatment**.

--

<br>

.large2[Accuracy is a property of the classifier. Bias is a property of the classifier
*and* the research design.]

--

<br>

You cannot read the second off the first. Ever.

---

# Note what the standard error does

Your `lm()` output for the middle case:

$$\hat\beta = 0.000, \quad \text{SE} = 0.008$$

--

<br>

A tight, precise, confidently estimated zero.

--

<br>

The 95% CI is $[-0.016, 0.016]$. It excludes the truth by a factor of six.

--

<br>

You would conclude the badge has no effect, and you would conclude it *precisely*.

---

# The general point

.large2[High accuracy plus systematic errors is more dangerous than low accuracy plus
random errors.]

--

<br>

Low accuracy makes you nervous. You go look.

--

93% accuracy makes you confident. You move on.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: corrections

# The corrections

---

# The good news

This is a solved problem. Three literatures converged on it in about eighteen months:
statistics, computer science, and econometrics.

--

<br>

They give you slightly different estimators with the same underlying logic.

--

<br>

.large2[Use a small set of gold-standard labels to correct the many machine labels.]

---

# The common structure

Every correction has the same shape:

--

$$\underbrace{\text{estimate from all } n \text{ machine labels}}_{\text{cheap, biased}} \;-\; \underbrace{\text{estimated bias from the } m \text{ gold labels}}_{\text{expensive, unbiased}}$$

--

<br>

The machine labels give you **precision**.

The human labels give you **validity**.

--

<br>

Neither alone is enough. You need both, and you need to know how the $m$ were drawn from
the $n$.

---

# Correction 1: design-based supervised learning

**Design-based supervised learning**, **DSL** from here on. Egami, Hinck, Stewart &
Wei (2023), *NeurIPS* 36.

--

<br>

Doubly robust estimator. Uses the surrogate labels everywhere, corrects them on a
random subsample where you have gold labels.

--

<br>

**The claim:** valid inference with **arbitrarily biased** surrogates.

--

<br>

Not "mildly biased." Arbitrarily. The LLM can be terrible and DSL still gives you a
consistent estimator and correct coverage.

---

# What DSL requires in exchange

.large2[You must **control and know** the probability that each document enters the
gold-standard sample.]

--

<br>

That is the whole trade.

--

<br>

"I labeled 500 reviews" is not enough. You need to be able to say: *each document had a
known probability $\pi_i$ of being sampled for human labeling, and here is how I set it.*

--

<br>

Simple random sampling works. Stratified works, if you know the strata probabilities.
Whatever you did on a Tuesday afternoon does not.

---

# DSL, practically

R package: `dsl`

Documentation: naokiegami.com/dsl/

--

<br>

```r
# not on CRAN
devtools::install_github("naoki-egami/dsl")
library(dsl)

out <- dsl(
  model   = "lm",
  formula = y ~ llm_label + x1 + x2,
  predicted_var = "llm_label",
  data    = df,        # all n rows
  sample_prob = "pi"   # your known sampling probability
)
```

--

<br>

The `sample_prob` argument is the whole lecture in one line of code.

--

If you cannot fill it in, you cannot use the method.

---

# Correction 2: prediction-powered inference

**Prediction-powered inference**, **PPI**. Angelopoulos, Bates, Fannjiang, Jordan &
Zrnic (2023),
*Science* 382(6671):669–674.

--

<br>

Same problem, statistics framing.

--

Small gold-standard sample + large set of machine predictions $\rightarrow$ confidence
intervals with **valid coverage**.

--

<br>

**No assumptions on the ML algorithm.** It can be a neural net, an LLM, a coin flip. The
guarantee does not depend on the predictor being any good.

--

<br>

It does assume **i.i.d. sampling** from a common distribution. Covariate shift and label
shift need separate results. So validate on the population you will analyze.

---

# PPI's logic

Compute your estimator two ways on the gold-standard sample:

1. Using the true labels
2. Using the machine labels

--

The difference is an estimate of the **rectifier**, how much the machine labels shift
your estimate.

--

<br>

Then: run the estimator on all $n$ machine labels, and subtract the rectifier.

--

<br>

$$\hat\theta_{\text{PPI}} = \hat\theta_{\text{machine}}(n) - \hat\Delta(m)$$

---

# When PPI helps, and when it doesn't

If the predictor is good, $\hat\Delta$ is small and you get big precision gains.

--

<br>

If it is bad, you can do **worse** than just using the gold sample alone.

--

<br>

The paper is explicit about this, there is a section called "Cases Where
Prediction-Powered Inference Is Underpowered."

--

The follow-up, **PPI++** (Angelopoulos et al., arXiv:2311.01453), adds power tuning
specifically to guarantee you never lose. If you use PPI, use PPI++.

---

# PPI, practically

Python package: `ppi_py`

--

<br>

```python
from ppi_py import ppi_ols_ci

ci = ppi_ols_ci(
    X_labeled,   Y_labeled,   Yhat_labeled,
    X_unlabeled, Yhat_unlabeled,
    alpha=0.05
)
```

--

<br>

Note the arguments. You need, on the labeled set, **both** the truth and the machine
prediction.

--

That means: run your LLM on the validation sample too. Do not skip this. People skip
this.

---

# Correction 3: the econometrics version

Battaglia, Christensen, Hansen & Sacher, "Inference for Regressions with Variables
Generated by AI or Machine Learning," arXiv:2402.15585 (working paper).

--

<br>

Same problem, our framing.

--

<br>

Treats the generated regressor as what it is: an estimated object with its own sampling
distribution. Gives bias-corrected estimators and standard errors that account for the
generation step.

--

<br>

If you have read the generated-regressors literature (Pagan 1984, Murphy & Topel 1985),
this will feel familiar. It is that idea, applied to ML-generated variables.

---

# Which one should you use?

For your project: **DSL**, unless you have a reason.

--

<br>

- It is in R
- The documentation is good
- The doubly-robust property is forgiving
- The interface forces you to state your sampling scheme, which is pedagogically the
  point

--

<br>

PPI if you are working in Python.

Battaglia et al. if your setting is a standard econometric model and you want the
econometrics-native treatment.

---

# The marketing application

Wang, Zhang & Zhang (2026), "Large Language Models for Market Research: A Data-Augmentation Approach: A
Data-Augmentation Approach," *Marketing Science* 45(4):728–751.

--

<br>

This is the paper to cite when a marketing referee asks whether this is a real problem
in *our* field.

--

<br>

Read it for the framing: LLM output as **augmentation** of a small human-labeled
dataset, not as a replacement for it.

--

<br>

That framing is correct and I want you to internalize it.

---

# The reframe

.large2[LLM labels are not data. They are a variance-reduction device applied to your
real data, which is the validation sample.]

--

<br>

Once you think of it this way, the design implications are obvious.

--

<br>

Which brings us to the part of the lecture that actually matters.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: design

# The design lesson

---

# What every correction needs

Look at what DSL, PPI, and Battaglia et al. have in common.

--

<br>

.large2[A validation sample whose sampling scheme **you controlled** and **you know**.]

--

<br>

Not a validation sample. *That* validation sample.

---

# The three things you need

1. A set of gold-standard labels
2. Known probability $\pi_i$ that each unit entered that set
3. LLM predictions on those same units

--

<br>

Miss any one and no correction applies.

--

<br>

Miss (2) specifically and you are in the most common failure mode I see: you have human
labels, you cannot use them, and you do not understand why.

---

# The failure I want to prevent

You annotate 50,000 documents in March.

You run your analysis in April.

--

You present in May, and someone asks about measurement error.

--

You go back in June and hand-label 500 documents "to validate."

--

<br>

.large2[Those 500 labels cannot fix your estimates.]

---

# Why not

Because you picked them in June, knowing what your results were.

--

<br>

- Did you sample them at random? From what frame?
- Did you oversample cases the model was uncertain about? (Reasonable! Also fatal, unless
  you know the probabilities.)
- Did you look at a few, find them boring, and go find more interesting ones?
- Did you stop when the accuracy number looked good?

--

<br>

Every one of those changes $\pi_i$, and you no longer know what $\pi_i$ was.

--

<br>

Without $\pi_i$ you can report an accuracy number. You cannot correct anything.

---

# The rule

.large2[The validation sample must be designed **before** you look at the results.]

--

<br>

Same logic as a pre-analysis plan. Same logic as not choosing your instrument after
seeing the first stage.

--

<br>

You already believe this about other parts of your design. Believe it about this one.

---

# You cannot bolt it on

There is no post-hoc fix.

--

There is no correction that recovers a sampling scheme you did not record.

--

There is no amount of compute that substitutes for 300 documents you should have labeled
in week two.

--

<br>

.large2[This is a **design** decision, not an **analysis** decision.]

---

# Which is why this is in a PhD course

If this were a software problem, I would send you a link to the `dsl` vignette and we
would be done in twenty minutes.

--

<br>

It is not a software problem. Running `dsl()` is trivial. Being *able* to run it requires
a decision you make months earlier, before you have any results, when it is not obvious
it will matter.

--

<br>

.large2[That is what methods training is for.]

--

<br>

The software will be different in three years. This will not be.

---

# What to do, concretely

**Before** you run the LLM on your full sample:

--

1. Decide how many documents you will hand-label. Budget for 300–1,000.

--

2. Decide the sampling scheme. Write it down. SRS is fine. Stratified is often better
   just record the strata and the probabilities.

--

3. Draw the sample. Save the indices. Save the seed.

--

4. Label them. Blind to model output if you can.

--

5. Run the LLM on the validation sample too, and keep those predictions.

--

<br>

Five steps. Two hours of thinking. It is the difference between a publishable design and
an unpublishable one.

---

# On sample size

How many gold labels?

--

<br>

The efficiency of these estimators depends on the gold sample. There is no universal
number, but as a working heuristic:

- **300** is a floor for a single binary construct
- **500–1,000** is where most published applications sit
- More if you have subgroups you need to be accurate within
- More if your construct is rare (you need enough positives)

--

<br>

If your construct occurs 2% of the time, a random sample of 500 gives you 10 positive
cases. That is not a validation study. Stratify.

---

# Stratified sampling is your friend

You are allowed to oversample.

--

<br>

Oversample rare positives. Oversample cases where the model is uncertain. Oversample your
treated group.

--

<br>

.large2[You just have to **know the probabilities** and pass them to the estimator.]

--

<br>

This is the same logic as survey weights. You already know how to do this. Nobody thinks
stratified sampling is cheating.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: leakage

# Training-data leakage

---

# A different problem

Everything so far has been about measurement error.

--

<br>

There is a second problem, orthogonal to the first, and it is easy to confuse them.

--

<br>

.small90[Ludwig, Mullainathan & Rambachan (2025), "Large Language Models: An Applied
Econometric Framework," NBER WP 33344.]

---

# Their contribution

They separate two things people mush together.

--

<br>

**Prediction problems.** You want the LLM's output to be a good forecast of something.

**Estimation / measurement problems.** You want the LLM's output to stand in for an
unobserved variable in a downstream estimate.

--

<br>

.large2[These need different assumptions, and satisfying one does not satisfy the other.]

---

# What each requires

**Prediction problems** require: *no training leakage*.

The LLM's training data must not contain the outcome you are predicting.

--

<br>

**Estimation problems** require: *a validation sample*.

Which is everything we just spent two hours on.

--

<br>

Clean separation. Know which problem you have.

---

# The leakage failure

You want to know whether news sentiment predicts stock returns.

--

You take news articles from 2022. You ask an LLM to rate sentiment. You regress 2022
returns on the rating.

--

<br>

Your model was trained on data through 2024.

--

<br>

.large2[It knows what happened.]

---

# Why no correction helps

The model does not need to reason about the article's tone. It can recall the outcome.

--

<br>

Your "sentiment measure" is partly a lookup of the realized return.

--

<br>

- Your $R^2$ is enormous
- Your validation sample agrees with the model, because *humans in 2024 also know*
- Every diagnostic looks great

--

<br>

.large2[This is a research-design problem. No statistical correction fixes it.]

--

DSL corrects for the model being *wrong*. It cannot correct for the model being *right for
the wrong reason*.

---

# When to worry

Ask: **could the model have memorized my outcome?**

--

<br>

Worry if:

- Your outcome is public and predates the training cutoff
- Your documents are famous (earnings calls, major news, well-known products)
- Your setting has been studied and the findings are on the internet
- You are "predicting" something that already happened

--

<br>

Worry less if:

- Your outcome is proprietary
- Your documents are obscure
- You are measuring a construct, not forecasting an event

---

# The diagnostic

Compare model performance on documents **before** and **after** the training cutoff.

--

<br>

If performance drops sharply after the cutoff, you have leakage in the pre-period.

--

<br>

Not a perfect test, the world also changes at the cutoff, but it is the standard check
and referees will expect it if your setting is exposed.

--

<br>

Report the model version and its training cutoff. Every time.

---

# The two-by-two

.small90[
| | No validation sample | Validation sample |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Leakage** | hopeless | still hopeless |
| **No leakage** | biased estimates | you're fine |
]

--

<br>

The top-right cell is the one people land in and don't realize.

--

You did the validation work. You ran the correction. And your measure is still a
memorized outcome.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: silicon

# Silicon sampling

---

# A different use of LLMs

Everything so far: LLM as a **labeler** of real data.

--

Now: LLM as a **respondent**. Simulated subjects. "Silicon sampling."

--

<br>

Shorter section. Same lesson, different clothes.

---

# The original claim

Argyle, Busby, Fulda, Gubler, Rytting & Wingate (2023), "Out of One, Many: Using Language
Models to Simulate Human Samples," *Political Analysis* 31(3):337–351.

--

<br>

Condition a language model on a demographic backstory. Ask it survey questions. Compare
to real survey respondents with the same demographics.

--

<br>

They call it **algorithmic fidelity**: the conditioned model reproduces the
distribution of human responses within demographic cells.

--

<br>

The result is real, and the paper is well done. It launched a literature.

---

# Why marketing got excited

Obvious appeal:

- Pretest surveys for free
- Simulate segments you cannot recruit
- Explore conjoint designs before fielding
- Scale qualitative research

--

<br>

If a model can stand in for a respondent, a large chunk of market research gets cheap.

---

# The rebuttal

Bisbee, Clinton, Dorff, Kenkel & Larson (2024), "Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey
Data? The Perils of Large Language Models," *Political Analysis* 32(4):401–416.

--

<br>

They replicate the exercise against ANES.

--

<br>

**Means:** ChatGPT recovers them well. Average feeling thermometers by group are close to
the real thing.

--

<br>

**Variance:** far too small.

---

# What too little variance does

Real respondents disagree. Within any demographic cell, human answers are spread out.

--

The LLM gives you the cell's modal answer, over and over, with too little dispersion
around it.

--

<br>

So the synthetic data has:

- approximately right first moments
- badly wrong second moments

--

<br>

.large2[Regression coefficients estimated on synthetic respondents differ significantly
from those estimated on real ones.]

---

# The teaching point

.large2[Matching first moments is not sufficient for valid inference.]

--

<br>

You do not estimate means. You estimate **relationships**.

--

Relationships live in the covariance structure. A method that gets the means right and
the covariances wrong is useless for your purpose and looks fine on the validation
exercise you were most likely to run.

--

<br>

If you validate a synthetic sample by checking group means, you have validated the one
thing that works.

---

# Note the structure

This is the same lecture again.

--

<br>

- Week 4: accuracy looked good $\rightarrow$ Week 5: the estimate was wrong
- Means look good $\rightarrow$ coefficients are wrong

--

<br>

.large2[The summary statistic that is easy to check is not the one your estimator depends
on.]

--

<br>

That sentence is the course.

---

# The marketing evidence: time preferences

Goli & Singh (2024), "Frontiers: Can Large Language Models Capture Human Preferences?"
*Marketing Science* 43(4):709–722.

--

<br>

They run intertemporal choice tasks, the standard "$X today vs. $Y in $t$ days"
elicitation, on LLMs and compare to human parameters.

--

<br>

**Finding:** LLMs are **less patient** than humans. Estimated discount rates are biased.

---

# Why this one is encouraging

The biases are **structured and detectable**.

--

<br>

Not random noise. A systematic deviation you can characterize, and in principle correct
for or condition on.

--

<br>

That is the useful version of a null result: it tells you the direction of the
problem.

--

<br>

Compare to "the LLM is sometimes wrong," which tells you nothing.

---

# The marketing evidence: willingness to pay

Brand, Israeli & Ngwe, "Using GPT for Market Research," HBS Working Paper 23-062.

--

<br>

They elicit willingness-to-pay from LLMs for product features.

--

<br>

**Works, with fine-tuning:** WTP within a product category the model was tuned on
including for **new features** in that category. Downward-sloping demand, sensible
orderings.

--

**Does not work:** extrapolating to a **new product category**, or across consumer
segments.

--

And the baseline matters: without fine-tuning, the authors report estimates that are
"often inaccurate and in some cases **wrong-signed**." 

---

# Why that split makes sense

Fine-tuning on human data from one category teaches the model that category's price
sensitivity. It can carry that to a new feature in the same category.

--

Move to a different category and there is nothing to carry. It produces something
plausible-sounding, which is exactly the failure mode with no signature.

--

<br>

.large2[LLMs interpolate their training distribution. They do not extrapolate outside
it.]

--

<br>

Which is a problem, because *new* is usually what marketing wants to know about.

---

# Where this leaves silicon sampling

I am not telling you not to do it. There is a real literature and real papers to write.

--

<br>

**Defensible uses:**
- Pretesting instruments and stimuli
- Generating hypotheses to test on humans
- Studying the LLM's behavior *as an object of interest*

--

**Not defensible yet:**
- Replacing a human sample and estimating a regression on synthetic respondents
- Any claim about a population the model has no basis for

--

<br>

And whatever you do: **validate on a real human sample**, and report the second moments,
not just the means.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: writing

# Writing the measurement section

---

# The practical close

You will write this section. Let's make it good.

--

<br>

Right now, most papers using LLM measurement have a measurement section that says:

> "We used GPT-4 to classify reviews. Accuracy against a hand-labeled sample was 89%."

--

<br>

Two sentences. That was enough in 2024.

--

<br>

.large2[It will not be enough when you go on the market.]

---

# What referees are learning to ask

The methodological literature is a year old. Referees are catching up now.

--

<br>

By the time your paper is under review, "89% accurate" will get you:

--

- "What was the sampling scheme for the validation set?"
- "Is classification error correlated with treatment?"
- "Report the confusion matrix, not just accuracy."
- "How do results change under DSL or PPI?"
- "What model version? What date? Is your outcome in its training data?"

--

<br>

I know these are coming because I am writing some of them.

---

# The checklist

**1. Report accuracy AND the confusion matrix.**

Accuracy alone hides the asymmetry that drives your bias. False positives and false
negatives affect your estimate differently. Give me the 2×2.

--

**2. State the sampling scheme for validation.**

How many, drawn how, with what probabilities, at what point in the project. One
paragraph. If you stratified, give the strata and the weights.

---

# The checklist

**3. Report naive AND corrected estimates side by side.**

Same table, adjacent columns. Let the reader see the size of the correction.

--

<br>

If they are similar: that is evidence for your design, and you should say so.

If they differ: you have found something, and hiding it will not work.

--

**4. Document model version and access date.**

`claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`, accessed 2026-03-14. Not "we used Claude."

The training cutoff too, if leakage is a concern in your setting.

---

# The checklist

**5. Save raw model outputs.**

Not the derived binary. The full response, the reasoning, the probability, the raw
string.

--

<br>

Three reasons:

- You will want to recode the construct later. You will.
- A referee will ask for a different threshold.
- When the model is deprecated, the raw outputs are the only thing left.

--

<br>

`prompts/` and the raw output files go in your repo. This is not optional in this course.

---

# A template

> We measure [construct] using [model version], accessed [date]. The full prompt is in
> Appendix X and the repository.
>
> To validate, we drew a [SRS / stratified] sample of $m$ = [N] documents, sampled with
> known probability [scheme], **before** running the model on the full corpus. Two coders
> labeled these independently ($\kappa$ = [X]).
>
> Agreement between the model and the gold standard is [X]%; the confusion matrix is in
> Table Y. Because classification error may be correlated with [treatment], we do not
> treat this as classical measurement error.
>
> We report both naive plug-in estimates and design-based corrected estimates (Egami et
> al. 2023) in Table Z.

--

<br>

Steal this. That is what it is for.

---

# One more thing

If your naive and corrected estimates are similar, **say so prominently**.

--

<br>

That is not a boring null. That is evidence that your measurement is not driving your
result. Which is the single thing a referee most wants to know.

--

<br>

.large2[The correction is not a hoop. It is an argument for your paper.]

---

# What I want you to take away

.large2[An 87% accurate instrument does not give you an 87% correct regression.]

--

<br>

.large2[Classification error is not classical, so "conservative" is not available.]

--

<br>

.large2[Every correction requires a validation sample you designed in advance.]

---
class: inverse, center, middle

# Where this leaves you

---

# Due this week

**Assignment 2**: the measurement pipeline. Due before next class.

--

<br>

**Week 5 milestone**, which is the one that matters:

--

1. Validation complete, gold labels drawn under a stated scheme, LLM run on the same
   units
2. Confusion matrix reported
3. **Naive and corrected estimates, side by side**

--

<br>

That third item is the deliverable. A milestone with only the naive estimate is
incomplete, and I will grade it that way.

---

# If you are stuck

Two failure modes I expect to see this week:

--

<br>

**"I already annotated everything and didn't draw a validation sample."**

Come talk to me. Depending on your setting we can sometimes draw a valid sample now. But
we need to do it before you look at any more results.

--

<br>

**"My construct is too rare for random sampling to work."**

Stratify. Bring me your sampling frame and we will design it together.

---

# Reading for next week

**Week 6: Credibility, design, specification search, experiments.**

--

<br>

We go back to identification. Given a measured variable you now trust, what makes the
comparison credible?

--

Specification search, multiple hypothesis testing, pre-registration, and what an
experiment buys you that an observational design does not.

--

<br>

It will feel like a more familiar course. It is also the week where I ask you the four
questions from Lecture 1 about *your own* project, out loud, in front of everyone.

---

# The thing I actually want you to remember

Your econometrics sequence taught you that measurement error is annoying but manageable,
and that the direction of the bias is usually known.

--

<br>

That was true for the measurement technologies it was built around.

--

<br>

.large2[It is not true for this one, and the profession has not fully absorbed that yet.]

--

<br>

You get to be early. Use it.

---
